data.title: Anthropic Vs. OpenAI: Who’s Winning The AI Race?
data.description:
Who’s Ahead in the Race Between Anthropic and OpenAI?

Key Takeaways

  • Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 leads the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 64.6 as of Nov. 17, 2026, ahead of OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra at 62.1.

  • Anthropic (ANT) has held the lead for seven consecutive months since April 2026, its longest stretch in front, after leadership changed hands eight times between September 2024 and April 2026.

  • The two companies released 13 frontier models in 2026 through mid-November, more than the 11 released in 2024 and 2025 combined.

The rivalry between Anthropic and OpenAI has become one of the defining competitions in artificial intelligence. Each new flagship model offers another chance to claim the top spot on AI intelligence benchmarks.

This graphic tracks the highest scores achieved by each company on the Artificial Analysis (AA) Intelligence Index over time. It includes Anthropic’s Opus and Fable models and OpenAI’s leading GPT and o-series models, showing only releases that set a new high for their company.

The index currently combines nine tests covering knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge. AA updated its methodology on Oct. 27, so scores before and after that date are not directly comparable.

Anthropic Has Had the Smartest AI Models Since April 2026

For much of the AI race, neither Anthropic nor OpenAI could hold onto the top spot for long. Between May 2025 and April 2026 alone, leadership changed seven times, with some advantages lasting only weeks.

That pattern changed when Anthropic’s Opus 4.7 overtook OpenAI in April 2026. Despite a steady stream of new releases from both companies, Anthropic has remained ahead on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index ever since.

The table below lists every model on the chart in order of release, along with its score on each version of the index:

Scores for models released before Opus 4.8 (May 2026) are Artificial Analysis estimates. Version 5.0.1 scores are shown for models plotted after the Oct. 27 methodology change.

Some victories in the AI race have been remarkably short-lived. Anthropic’s Opus 4.5 held the lead for just 17 days before OpenAI’s GPT-5.2 overtook it in December 2025.

The longer-term picture is more balanced than the current streak suggests. Since March 2024, Anthropic has spent 529 days in front, compared with 459 days for OpenAI. That makes its current run especially significant in a competition where leadership has historically been difficult to maintain.

Anthropic’s lead also survived AA’s Oct. 27 update, which added two tests, upgraded three, and removed three.

However, different benchmarks can produce different winners. On Epoch AI’s Capabilities Index, OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra leads with a score of 174.2, narrowly ahead of Fable 5.2 at 173.5. The difference falls within both models’ margins of error.

Frontier AI Model Releases Have Doubled in Pace This Year

The competition has also accelerated. In 2025, Anthropic and OpenAI released a new frontier model roughly every 52 days. In 2026, that interval has shortened to about 25 days, with 13 releases through mid-November.

Anthropic has driven much of that pace, accounting for eight of the 13 releases this year. OpenAI has often responded within days. GPT-6 Astra arrived two days after Fable 5.1 and scored 0.7 points lower. In November, GPT-6.2 Astra followed Fable 5.2 by eight days and finished 2.4 points behind.

But benchmark leadership is only one measure of success. OpenAI also faces growing competition in the broader AI chatbot market, where user adoption tells a different story.

ChatGPT accounted for 88% of global AI chatbot website traffic at the end of 2024, but its share fell to 56% by September 2026 as Anthropic’s Claude and Google (GOOGL) Gemini gained ground.

data.title: Would The Fed Hike Interest Rates In A Month Where The CPI Is Negative?
data.description:
We may find out in December.

The Fed meets on December 9, 2026.

It is a near certainty the Fed hikes interest rates. Call it 99+ percent.

Despite a lot of chatter about a 50 basis point hike, that’s not going to happen no matter how bad the PCE report is on November 26.

Question of the Day

Negative CPI Reading Quite Possible

Energy prices will decline.

And if there is very tame Owners’ Equivalent Rent (OER) it can easily happen.

Shelter is over 35 percent of the CPI with OER nearly 26 percent. Energy was 7.65 percent of the CPI in October.

If shelter comes in flat, and energy is down big, we are going to see a negative CPI reading the day after the Fed hikes.

Energy Q&A With Grok

Mish: What is the projection for the energy component of the CPI report for November?

Grok: Projections for the energy component of the November 2026 CPI (due for release December 10, 2026) point to a significant decline, on the order of roughly −2.5% month-over-month. globalmacrolens.com

The most detailed publicly available nowcast comes from GlobalMacroLens (updated as of November 19, 2026). It estimates the energy component at −2.53% m/m (weight ~7.2%), contributing about −0.184 percentage points to headline CPI.

This is derived from weekly EIA fuel prices (among other free public data) to bridge the energy leaves of the CPI basket. The same nowcast puts headline CPI at about +0.04% m/m (3.9% y/y) and core at +0.25% m/m (2.9% y/y). globalmacrolens.com

Prediction markets (e.g., Kalshi) price headline around −0.1% m/m / 3.7% y/y.

GlobalMacroLens Baseline

What Would It Take to Go Negative?

You only need roughly another −0.05 pp of contribution to reach something like −0.01% (or a bit more for a clearer negative print).

  • Energy alone: An extra ~0.7 percentage-point decline (i.e., energy around −3.2% to −3.5% m/m instead of −2.5%) would do it, all else equal. That is plausible if the late-month gasoline drop is a bit steeper than the weekly EIA data already embedded in the nowcast.

  • Shelter help: Because of its high weight, a 0.1 pp slower shelter reading (e.g., +0.15–0.20% instead of the recent ~0.3% pace) adds roughly another −0.035 pp of drag.

  • Combination (the most realistic path): Energy at roughly −3.0% m/m + shelter closer to +0.15–0.20% (or even just a bit softer than the +0.29% core-services assumption) easily clears the zero line. Food or core-goods softness would help further but is not required.

Grok Comment: This lines up with market pricing (Kalshi median around −0.1% m/m) and commentary noting that the sharp gasoline/oil drop is the main swing factor for a soft headline print. Shelter is slower-moving and less likely to surprise dramatically to the downside in a single month, so the energy outcome is the bigger variable.

Genuine Tossup

I give a lot of credence to the betting markets.

So, I am upping my 35 percent chance off the top of my head answer to Michael Lebowitz.

I now think a Fed hike in a month with a negative CPI reading is a genuine tossup, if not slightly odds on.

Note that the BLS rounds to a single digit. Thus -0.049 would get rounded to 0.0.

I calculate to two digits. If the judge is a two digit calculation, I think the odds are 60 percent that the discussed event occurs. Otherwise, flip a coin.

This was the third consecutive bad month for CPI inflation.

November 18, 2026: Only One Republican Senator Opposes Wasting $450 Billion More in Iran

Rand Paul blasts Republican warmongering priorities in the lame duck Session.

“The American public is going to see this as financing the Iran war. It will lead to more inflation”

“At this point, the entire fiscal conservative movement in the Senate is only me.”

data.title: Anthropic's ANT Closes At $97.17, Up 17% On Its First Day Of Trading
data.description:
Anthropic’s Class A shares, ticker ANT, closed at $97.17 on their first day on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on 19 November 2026.

That is about 17% above the $83.00 IPO price set a day earlier, and about 13% below the $111.50 opening print.

The day began in Times Square, where co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei rang the Nasdaq opening bell at 9:30am ET. The ceremony itself did not start trading in ANT. The first trade came later, at 16:50 GMT (11:50am ET), when the shares opened at $111.50, about 34% above the offering price.

Indications had been climbing through the morning, from about $99.60 to $105, then $110 and $111, before the stock opened slightly above that last level. The early burst did not last.

ANT peaked at $115.10 just before noon ET and slipped as low as $92.72.

By mid-afternoon the shares were changing hands around $95.60, still about 15% above the IPO price. The $97.17 close left the debut comfortably above the offering, but well short of the opening pop.

Even so, a 17% first-day gain on the largest IPO on record is a strong debut, the more so on a session in which the main US indexes finished more than 2% lower. The market took some of the opening froth off, but buyers who received stock at $83 still ended the day well in the money.

More than 846 million shares changed hands, ahead of the 522 million traded on SpaceX’s opening day in June, and enough to make ANT the most actively traded name on the Nasdaq. Volume had already passed 640 million by mid-session.

At the $111.50 open, Reuters put Anthropic’s market value at about $2 trillion, a level exceeded by only a handful of US-listed firms, and ahead of the $1.96 trillion it assigned to SpaceX at its June opening trade. That is a reported valuation at the open, not a closing figure.

The fade came as the wider market turned lower. US stocks ended more than 2% down. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 1,101.11 points, or 2.19%, to 49,097.06, the S&P 500 fell 2.02% to 7,175.83, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.25% to 23,879.20.

AI shares were mixed as investors weighed worries about higher interest rates. The Nasdaq itself had been up as much as 2% after the open before those gains were given back.

The listing is the first by a frontier AI lab and sets a public-market benchmark for the group, with OpenAI still private. Ordinary investors now have a listed way to take a direct view on a stand-alone model developer, rather than only through the chipmakers and cloud groups that have dominated the trade.

Anthropic sold 980 million Class A shares at $83.00 on Wednesday, of which 956,351,354 were sold by the company and 23,648,646 by selling stockholders. The deal raised about $81.3 billion, making it the largest initial public offering on record, above SpaceX’s initial $75 billion.

The size and price had already been lifted once before the open. Last week the company had marketed 825 million shares at $70 to $78; on Wednesday it sold more stock, and at a higher price, than that range implied. SpaceX later reached $85.7 billion after its overallotment was exercised.

Anthropic’s underwriters have the option to buy up to a further 147 million Class A shares, which would bring in another $12.2 billion and take the IPO total to $93.5 billion if exercised. They have until 20 November to take up that option. The offering itself is expected to close on 20 November, subject to customary conditions.

The banks on the deal are due about $550 million in underwriting fees, according to the company’s filing, more than the roughly $500 million paid on the SpaceX IPO.

The company priced the offering above its marketed range and increased the number of shares being sold, initially valuing the Claude developer at $1.5 trillion. Investors who received an allocation pay the $83 offering price. Anyone buying once the shares are listed pays the market price, which closed at $97.17.

Demand was unusually lopsided. Retail interest in the IPO was the largest in history. Anthropic prioritized institutional investors it already knew, and roughly half of the firms that placed orders were left empty-handed, a higher share than usual.

Retail allocation came in at around 15%, below the roughly 20% the company had targeted, though still above the 5% to 10% typical in most IPOs.

Analysts who opened coverage stayed above the close. Melius started at Buy with a $155 price target; Ben Reitzes, the firm’s head of technology research, said that assigned value could even be “conservative”. Needham’s Scott Berg has a Buy rating and a $150 target. The average target across five Buy ratings was about $116.

Wolfe Research, in a Thursday note, said cybersecurity could match Anthropic’s coding opportunity and reach $500 billion annually.

The company has given a sense of the scale behind that interest. In its prospectus, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion of revenue in the nine months to 30 September, up about 1,200% from the same period a year earlier, and that its run-rate revenue was about $81 billion by the end of October.

What comes next is tightly timetabled. Index funds will not add the stock immediately. The Morningstar US Total Market Index will include it after five trading days, the Nasdaq-100 after 18 December, and the S&P 500 will not add it for at least a year.

About 15.5 billion insider shares are subject to lock-up agreements that run until after Anthropic reports results in the third quarter of next year. No date has been set for the first earnings report.

The official terms of the offering are in our report on Anthropic’s official IPO pricing. The first print is covered in our report on how ANT opened.

The wider timetable is on our Anthropic IPO date, valuation and ticker hub. For access and why the open-market price is not $83, see how to buy Anthropic stock.

data.title: AMD Stock Falls 7% As Hunterbrook Alleges Links To Blacklisted Chinese Firm
data.description:
AMD stock fell 7% on Thursday after Hunterbrook Media, an investigative publication affiliated with short seller Hunterbrook Capital, alleged that the chipmaker's firmware was being used by a blacklisted Chinese company and three businesses linked to it.

The report claimed that IEIT Systems, a Chinese server maker, had incorporated at least six newer versions of AMD's firmware into its products after being placed on the US government's export blacklist.

Hunterbrook also alleged that three other server companies with links to IEIT offered products containing closely matching firmware, raising questions about whether servers designed by the blacklisted company were being sold through other businesses.

The revelations were made in a report called 'AMD has its own China problem'.

Hunterbrook Media disclosed that, at the time of publication, its affiliated investment firm Hunterbrook Capital was short AMD shares and held long positions in a basket of comparable securities.

The report drew parallels with the controversy surrounding Nvidia's (NVDA) sales of advanced chips to Chinese companies and questioned whether AMD could genuinely be considered a safer alternative to its larger rival.

AMD's China exposure comes under scrutiny

The firm has questioned a growing perception that AMD is a less risky way to gain exposure to the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom amid scrutiny of Nvidia's China business.

The firm highlighted that AMD shares gained nearly 45% in the five sessions through November 12, the day Nvidia announced CEO Jensen Huang's resignation in what CNBC reported was a board decision to oust him.

William Blair and Oppenheimer also upgraded AMD during that period, according to Hunterbrook.

However, the publication argued that investors may be underestimating AMD's exposure to the same geopolitical and regulatory risks facing Nvidia.

As of the November 18 close, AMD traded at around 30 times its estimated earnings for the next fiscal year, compared with approximately nine times for Nvidia, based on analyst estimates published by Yahoo Finance.

"The Bear Cave believes investors are trading one cousin’s problems for the other’s," the report said, referring to Jensen Huang's relationship with AMD chief Lisa Su, who is his cousin.

The Bear Cave is an investigative newsletter owned by Hunterbrook Media.

IEIT allegedly used AMD firmware after blacklisting

Hunterbrook said the US Commerce Department placed IEIT on its Entity List in March 2025.

The designation means that exports of items covered by US export controls to the company require a licence, with the department's stated policy being to deny such applications.

Despite the restrictions, IEIT has incorporated at least six newer versions of AMD's firmware into its products since being blacklisted, according to the investigation.

The latest version identified by Hunterbrook appeared in an updated product listing posted on October 19.

The report also identified three companies that sell servers built around AMD chips under their own brands: Maginfra in China, Kaytus in Singapore and Aivres in California.

"Hunterbrook found that the firmware they offer is nearly identical to IEIT’s, suggesting they may be selling servers designed by the blacklisted company. Corporate filings point the same way: IEIT’s 2022 annual report listed Aivres, then called Inspur Systems, as a subsidiary. Kaytus’s own audited accounts name IEIT as its ultimate parent company," it said.

The investigation also highlighted other alleged links between AMD and entities subject to US restrictions.

Hunterbrook said AMD reported $67 million in licensing income in 2025 that the publication traced to two Chinese chip ventures blacklisted in 2019.

It also identified a server from Cancon, an alias of the blacklisted company Suma, in AMD's February 2026 product catalogue.

"In sum: AMD appears no less at risk from China chip restrictions than Nvidia, despite the recent surge of positive coverage," Hunterbrook said.

Potential changes to export rules could add pressure

The report also warned that changes to US export regulations could expose AMD to additional restrictions on its international business.

A suspension of a rule that would extend export restrictions to foreign companies at least 50% owned by blacklisted entities is due to expire on January 10, 2027.

If implemented, the provision could expand restrictions to Kaytus and other foreign companies in which IEIT holds at least a 50% stake, it said.

Separately, a newly released interim final rule, which takes effect on Thursday, will require licences for advanced chips shipped to Singapore and four other countries.

The potential impact on AMD could be significant given its business in the region.

The company recorded $4.28 billion in billings to customers in Singapore during fiscal 2025, accounting for more than 10% of its total sales.

"For AMD, this could mean additional licensing requirements that can delay or block sales," Hunterbrook said.

data.title: Why The Biggest IPO Ever Matters For Gold Investors
data.description:
On October 29, I wrote that when gold falls on supportive news, the sellers are in control. Gold is about $300 lower now.

At the moment of writing these words, December gold futures trade near $3,720, after moving down to $3,694.50 overnight, their lowest level since September 2, 2025. Silver futures trade near $45, and the GDXJ, the ETF for junior mining stocks, closed at $90.07 on Wednesday, its lowest close since November 2025. Meanwhile, the stock futures are higher ahead of the debut of Anthropic, whose IPO is the biggest on record.

The rule about the sellers works in the stock market too, and Wednesday showed it. 

Stocks Ignored the Best News of the Week

On October 29, when December gold futures traded near $4,033, I wrote: "When gold falls on a day that should support it, the sellers are in control. In my view, this is bearish information." Since then, gold has declined by about 8 percent.

On Wednesday, stocks had every reason to rally. Nvidia's (NVDA) revenue rose 103 percent from a year earlier and beat expectations; Target (TGT) and Lowe's (LOW) beat expectations as well, oil fell, and the 10-year Treasury yield slipped to 5.06 percent. The S&P 500 fell anyway. It lost 0.23 percent, to 7,323.63, its fifth decline in a row and its lowest close since July 29. The sellers are in control of stocks too, and this matters for the stock market's relationship with gold, because the miners are stocks as well.

It's also notable that the S&P 500 isn't soaring from its lows the way it did before. In late July, it gained 1.66 percent on the day after its July 29 close. In early November, it soared on the third day: after the lows of November 5 and 6, it gained 2.35 percent on November 9. This morning, the S&P 500 futures are up about 1.2 percent, which isn't much after five declines in a row.

Tech stocks are holding up better. On Wednesday, the Nasdaq 100 gained 0.42 percent, while the S&P 500 lost 0.23 percent, and this morning, the Nasdaq 100 futures are up about 2 percent. In my view, this could be based on the hype around Anthropic's (ANT) IPO, and it could be overstated.

That hype deserves a closer look, because hyped listings have a track record. 

What Hyped Listings Have Told Us About Tops

On Wednesday evening, Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, above the $70-78 range, at a valuation of about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis. Its shares start trading on Nasdaq today under the ticker ANT.

SpaceX (SPCX) is the freshest example of what came next in such cases. It priced its IPO at $135 on June 11 and reached $225.64 on June 16, its third day of trading. That was the top. By mid-July, SpaceX traded below its IPO price, and on Wednesday, it closed at $143.50, about 36 percent below the June high.

Silver did the same in 2006, when the first big silver ETF was launched. The iShares Silver Trust (SLV) started trading on April 28, 2006. Silver kept rallying for less than two weeks, and the gain was less than 20 percent. It topped on May 11, and within about a month, it fell about 35 percent.

There are more examples. Palm's (PALMV) IPO in March 2000 came 6 trading days before the Nasdaq's record close at the peak of the dot-com bubble, and the index then lost 78 percent. Rivian's (RIVN) IPO in November 2021 came 7 trading days before the Nasdaq's record close of that cycle.

Not every hyped listing marks the top of the entire market. After SpaceX's IPO, the Nasdaq Composite kept rising until its October 6 record. Anthropic, though, is listing into a market that's already falling: the Nasdaq 100 closed on Wednesday about 13 percent below its October 6 record, and Nvidia closed at its lowest level since June 2025 despite beating expectations. 

Why Hyped Listings Tend to Come Near Tops

There are three reasons. The first is new supply. Anthropic's IPO and private placement brought $107.3 billion of new shares to the market, five months after SpaceX's $75 billion IPO set the previous record, and to buy the new shares, many investors sell other stocks. The second is that insiders choose when to sell. Companies and their early investors go public when buyers are willing to pay the most, which is why IPOs cluster after strong markets. The third is that nobody might be left to buy. Those who want the hyped stock buy it in the first days, and after that, the sellers take over.

In my view, this IPO might be happening at the peak of the AI hype or right after it peaked, and it could be the final moment when the enthusiasm peaks. Anthropic's valuation of about $1.5 trillion is up from $965 billion in its private funding round in May. It might not be realistic, and investors might realize that and sell the stock, even though AI technology is revolutionary.

If that happens, the miners are likely to feel it first. 

Why the Miners Fall Harder

When stocks decline, the mining stocks tend to fall more than gold, because investors sell them as stocks first and as gold proxies second. On Wednesday, the GDXJ fell 6.02 percent, almost twice as much as gold, on a day when the S&P 500 lost only 0.23 percent.

On October 26, after gold slipped below $4,000, I wrote: "Until the miners start rising on gold's down days, or at least falling less than gold, I think the decline in the sector has further to go." Since then, the GDXJ has lost about 9 percent, and gold about 7 percent. The miners are still falling more than gold, and on Wednesday, the GDXJ broke down to new 2026 lows, also in terms of the closing prices.

Gold itself reached an important level overnight. 

Gold Reaches Its Declining Support Line

On September 10, when gold traded near $4,400, I wrote that a daily close below the neckline of gold's head-and-shoulders top, then near $4,320, "would complete the formation with its target below $4,000." Since then, gold has declined by about 15 percent.

Now, gold has moved down to its declining support line, and such gold support levels often slow a decline, so a pause is possible here, also in silver and the mining stocks.

One of my Gold Trading Alerts subscribers asked in the comments whether I expect any rally attempts before gold reaches about $3,500. It's a good question, and I'm happy to answer it here as well. In short, a pause is possible here, but I don't expect a meaningful rally before the next leg lower. In April 2013, no consolidation followed the breakdown: gold crashed 10.8 percent to its April 16 low, and the 12.6 percent correction came only after that. In my view, a sizable gold price correction is more likely to start from lower prices than from current prices. On a side note, I just updated my final downside target for gold - $3,500 is just the first one.

Before I sum up, there's one more thing worth celebrating today. 

Happy International Men's Day

Today, November 19, is International Men's Day. Dr. Jerome Teelucksingh from Trinidad and Tobago first celebrated it in 1999, and it's now marked in more than 80 countries. The day celebrates the positive value that men bring to the world, their families and their communities, and this year's theme is "The Future Is Everyone."

To all the men reading this: Happy International Men's Day! I wish you good health, strength and plenty of time with the people who matter most to you. If there's a check-up that you've been postponing, today is a good day to book it. You are important. And if that doesn’t convince you, think of your body as a business asset – you don’t want it to depreciate too fast… And to all the women reading this: thank you for celebrating with us. 

Where This Leaves Us

The stock market ignored the best news of the week, and today, the biggest IPO on record debuts into a market that's already falling. Hyped listings have often come near tops, and when stocks decline, the miners tend to fall harder than gold. Gold reached its declining support line, so a pause is possible here, but in my view, gold is likely to decline to at least $3,500. In today's Gold Trading Alert, I also updated my long-term gold chart and my view on where this decline is most likely to end, and I described my plan for the next two trades.

When the last buyers are in, the hype ends, and the miners are usually the first to feel it.

data.title: The S&P 500 Breaks Support As Global Risk Sentiment Begins To Crack
data.description:
Stocks finished sharply lower, down about 2% on the S&P 500 and more than 2% on the NASDAQ 100. Anthropic (ANT) made its market debut, opening around $111.50 after pricing at $83, and closed the day around $97. I’m not surprised to see the stock close lower than the opening price, given the lock-up release discussed last weekend. Tomorrow will be an interesting day to see how it trades.

The S&P 500 index opened higher and traded up to around 7,400, but selling took over for the rest of the session, and it finished at 7,175. Support at 7,300 has now broken, leaving a thin shelf of support between 7,070 and 7,130. If that breaks, it opens the path to around 6,750, which dates back to a gap created in early April.

As the chart shows, support is thin once the index breaks below 7,070.

Tomorrow is monthly OPEX, and once we get past the morning expiration on the open, the put wall falls from 7,100 to 7,000 and stays there through Monday. That takes the shelf out from under the 7,070 to 7,130 support band, so if the index wants to drop after the open, there is room for it.

It is also worth pointing out that despite volatility staying elevated, we are not getting the volatility crush we would normally expect once event risk has passed. That makes me think something deeper is going on, and that something in this market has changed.

As I pointed out a long time ago, AUD/JPY is an important FX pair and closely tied to risk sentiment. We are now seeing it not only break support at 108, but head lower from there. That is starting to signal a shift in global risk sentiment and a broader move out of risk.

If this is a broader risk-off shift in global markets, the bigger question is whether an unwind of the carry trade that Japan’s low rates have fueled is driving it. We don’t know yet, but it is something we must watch.

data.title: Wall Street Chokes On Anthropic As The AI Trade Comes Unstuck
data.description:
The liquidity arithmetic was hard to ignore. Anthropic (ANT) raised $81.3 billion through its public offering, or $107.3 billion including the $26 billion strategic private placement, while the S&P 500 shed approximately $1.3 trillion in market value during the session. Those numbers aren’t directly comparable, and they certainly don’t establish that IPO funding caused the equity losses. But they capture the uncomfortable optics of a market trying to absorb an enormous new asset while everything surrounding it was being marked down.

Takeaways by Dark Side of the Boom

• The biggest IPO in history delivered a spectacular opening, but Wall Street couldn’t swallow the supply without choking on the rest of the market.

• Anthropic’s success exposed an increasingly uncomfortable divide between investors willing to pay for frontier AI and those still financing the infrastructure beneath it.

• A heavily short gamma market turned an ordinary sell the news reversal into a disorderly liquidation, with options hedging pouring fuel on the fire.

• King Dollar and Treasuries found buyers as equities, precious metals and crypto buckled, leaving Friday’s options expiration as the next potential turning point.

Wall Street Chokes on Anthropic

Wall Street rolled out the red carpet for Anthropic, uncorked the champagne and promptly gagged on the biggest IPO in history. What began as a celebration of artificial intelligence ended with the S&P 500 down 2%, the Nasdaq swinging from gains of more than 2% to losses of roughly the same magnitude, and more than 460 members of the benchmark retreating. The S&P has now fallen for six consecutive sessions, its longest losing streak since April 2024, while the Dow is knocking on the door of a technical correction. For a market supposedly desperate to rediscover its AI mojo, this was an extraordinarily expensive way to demonstrate enthusiasm.

Some context: the S&P 500 lost around $1.3 trillion in market cap today as Anthropic's IPO went out around $1.3 trillion.

Anthropic itself wasn’t the problem, at least not in the conventional sense. The stock opened at $111.50 against its $83 IPO price, an immediate premium of more than 34%, before sellers descended and whittled the advance to roughly 17% by the close. That still leaves the Claude developer with a fully diluted valuation approaching $1.8 trillion, putting it among the ten largest public companies on the planet. The IPO was a triumph for the underwriters and early shareholders. Unfortunately, the rest of Wall Street appeared to have been invited to the party mainly to pick up the bill.

The timing was almost comical. Equity futures rallied overnight on expectations that Anthropic would restore confidence in the AI complex, only for the broader market to begin losing altitude as the opening indication for ANT climbed. Then came reports that many institutional investors had received little or no allocation. Whether that reflected overwhelming demand or an unusually concentrated distribution, it left the market trying to price a record offering against a backdrop of increasingly fragile risk appetite.

And once ANT began trading around midday, the wheels really came off.

The Biggest IPO Meets Wall Street’s Worst Positioning

The problem wasn’t simply that investors decided to sell the news. The market was carrying a particularly nasty options configuration into the session, with dealers reportedly holding their largest short gamma exposure since 2019. Nomura’s Charlie McElligott had already flagged the dangerous collision between Nvidia, Anthropic and November options expiration, and Thursday delivered the sort of violent price action that makes dealers wish they’d taken the afternoon off.

Short gamma doesn’t tell you which direction the market will travel. It tells you how quickly things can get ugly once it chooses one. When dealers are short gamma, their hedging tends to reinforce the prevailing move, buying into rallies and selling into declines. Had the opening enthusiasm survived, the same machinery could have helped launch a spectacular squeeze. Instead, equities rolled over, zero-day options activity amplified the afternoon decline, and the hedging machinery began feeding the very weakness it was supposed to manage.

There was plenty of dry tinder. Goldman’s prime brokerage data showed hedge funds carrying technology exposure of roughly 18% against an index weight near 29%, an extraordinary 11-percentage-point underweight. On paper, that left enormous room for a rally if investors were forced to chase performance. But underweight investors aren’t necessarily eager buyers when the market starts falling through the floor. The hoped-for squeeze never arrived, leaving sellers with precious little resistance.

The damage spread well beyond the obvious AI names. The Magnificent Seven surrendered their early gains, neocloud stocks went from roughly 6% higher to 4% lower, and all eleven S&P sectors finished in the red. The VIX approached 28, volatility of volatility climbed above 125, and rising implied correlation suggested that investors were no longer distinguishing much between winners and losers. The market was selling risk rather than carefully selecting casualties.

And the liquidity arithmetic was hard to ignore. Anthropic raised $81.3 billion through its public offering, or $107.3 billion including the $26 billion strategic private placement, while the S&P 500 shed approximately $1.3 trillion in market value during the session. Those numbers aren’t directly comparable, and they certainly don’t establish that IPO funding caused the equity losses. But they capture the uncomfortable optics of a market trying to absorb an enormous new asset while everything surrounding it was being marked down.

The money had to come from somewhere. And judging by the performance of Nvidia (NVDA), copper, gold, and crypto, investors weren’t exactly reaching into their spare-change jars.

The AI Winner Takes the Money, but the Builders Take the Beating

The more revealing fault line is emerging between the businesses developing frontier AI models and the sprawling infrastructure trade that finances their ambitions.

Anthropic’s debut demonstrates that investors remain willing to pay extraordinary prices for a leading model developer. What it doesn’t establish is that the market has rediscovered an unlimited appetite for debt-heavy cloud operators, semiconductor suppliers and the financing arrangements supporting the AI construction boom.

That’s a much tougher proposition, especially as interest rates climb and credit investors become more discriminating.

AMD (AMD) was caught in a separate storm after Hunterbrook Capital disclosed a short position and raised allegations involving China-related risks and financing arrangements. AMD denied wrongdoing, but the stock was hammered nonetheless. New US chip licensing restrictions also pressured Taiwan Semiconductor-exposed companies and Asian data-centre names, adding another layer of uncertainty to an industry already struggling to defend its capital spending assumptions.

Credit markets reflected the broader discomfort. Investment-grade and high-yield spreads swung sharply before finishing wider across sectors, although hyperscaler and data-centre credit held up somewhat better than the equity carnage might suggest.

The distinction between buying a successful AI model developer and underwriting the entire infrastructure race is becoming increasingly important. Anthropic can attract a mountain of equity capital without proving that every supplier, neocloud operator and leveraged data-centre project deserves its previous valuation.

Wall Street appears increasingly willing to finance the perceived winners while demanding a much harder reckoning from everyone selling them the shovels.

Meanwhile, the dollar and Treasuries offered the usual escape routes from a badly bruised equity market. The ten-year Treasury yield drifted back toward 5%, even as crude oil edged higher following renewed attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz. The historic Trump-Xi-Putin summit in Shenzhen produced a declaration supporting increased refined petroleum supply, but the oil market appeared more interested in physical security than diplomatic choreography.

King Dollar extended its advance to seven of the past eight sessions, reaching fresh 18-month highs as high-beta currencies came under pressure. The Colombian peso and offshore yuan were among the casualties of a broader carry unwind, while gold slipped below $3,700 for the first time since September 2025. Bitcoin (BTC.X) suffered another ugly round trip, retreating toward its July lows.

When bonds and the dollar are attracting money while gold, crypto and equities are being liquidated together, the market is telling you that immediate liquidity has become more valuable than long-term investment narratives.

And that’s where Friday’s options expiration becomes particularly important.

The S&P 500 has now slipped further below its 200-day moving average (nothing good happens when any asset slips below the 200-day Dark Side of the Boom), with the sixth consecutive decline adding an uncomfortable technical dimension to the fundamental debate.

Historical comparisons offer some consolation: on the three previous occasions over the past 30 years when the index posted six straight declines while finishing less than 3% below its 200-day average, equities were higher five sessions later. Unfortunately, each episode was followed by more substantial downside.

With the S&P’s intraday low near 7,193, the 7,000–7,100 area being watched by technical traders is beginning to look considerably less remote.

Friday’s expiration could release some of the negative gamma that helped turn Thursday’s reversal into a rout, potentially allowing the market to stabilise heading toward Thanksgiving. But that would resolve a mechanical pressure point, not the wider argument about AI profitability, borrowing costs and the increasingly selective appetite for technology risk.

Anthropic’s first session proved that Wall Street still has an enormous appetite for the AI crown jewels. The trouble is that investors seem increasingly willing to sell the rest of the kingdom to pay for them. And after Thursday’s spectacular failure to sustain an opening rally, I’d be watching what happens to Nvidia and the broader technology complex after the options machinery resets, rather than taking comfort from another impressive print in ANT.

data.title: XEQT Vs GEQT: Which All-In-One ETF Fits Your Retirement?
data.description:
XEQT holds about ten times as many companies as GEQT. GEQT puts 64% of its money in two sectors. And its largest position, Nvidia (NVDA), weighs almost twice as much as it does in XEQT.

Both are all-in-one ETFs. Both are 100% stocks. They are not the same bet.

Here is my take before we start. One is a broad market investment. The other is a big bet on tech and financials, even though it is built around your values.

Here is the full comparison on video if you would rather watch it than read it.

What Are XEQT and GEQT?

Two all-in-one equity ETFs. XEQT buys the world, with 8,000 to 9,000 stocks. GEQT is an ESG-screened version with about 800 stocks and no emerging markets.

The idea is the same for both. You buy one ETF, it holds a basket of country ETFs, and it rebalances automatically.

XEQT touches Canada, the US, international and emerging markets. You are everywhere. Almost too much everywhere, because you reach up to 9,000 companies.

GEQT has a similar structure, with one ETF per region. The most important difference is that it is ESG screened: environmental, social and good governance. It excludes fossil fuels, among other things.

One note on that. Read the rules and look at the companies. Whether a stock qualifies as ESG is debatable and depends on your point of view and values.

XEQT vs GEQT: two all-in-one ETFs, two strategies

How Do XEQT and GEQT Compare Side by Side?

Fees and yield are close. Size is not. XEQT has $23.6 billion in net assets and GEQT about $311 million.

Fees: XEQT charges a management fee of 0.17%, reduced in late 2025, and GEQT 0.22%. With the underlying ETFs included, the MER is 0.19% and 0.25%. On $100,000, that is $190 against $250 a year, a $60 gap. Nothing to write home about.

Trailing yield: 1.61% for XEQT and 1.16% for GEQT. Both are low-yield, high-growth products. You will not make a difference here either.

Underlying companies: this is where they split. XEQT holds between 8,000 and 9,000 stocks. GEQT holds about 800.

Net assets: $23.6 billion for XEQT, a popular ETF. About $311 million for GEQT. Not the same ballpark.

Inception: August 2019 for XEQT, September 2020 for GEQT. That gives a little over five years to compare returns. Useful, but not a long track record.

XEQT vs GEQT fees, yield and size, BlackRock data as of November 3, 2026

Where Do They Invest?

Mostly in North America. About 70% for XEQT and 77% for GEQT.

Both hold between 40% and 45% in US stocks. Canada is 25% in XEQT and 31% in GEQT. International markets take 23% of GEQT, with no exposure to emerging markets. XEQT holds more international and adds emerging markets.

So with either one, you are basically investing in North America.

XEQT vs GEQT geographic allocation

How Concentrated Is GEQT?

Very. Technology and financials each take 32% of GEQT, for 64% of the portfolio. In XEQT, those two sectors add up to 44%.

The sectors were the biggest surprise. GEQT has 0% in energy, as you would expect. Then technology at 32% and financials at 32%.

Technology and financials are doing well right now. That’s great. I am still not sure you want two-thirds of your portfolio in two sectors.

At DSR, we flag any sector above 20%. XEQT sits right around that line with technology at 22% and financials at 21%. After that, it spreads out: industrials at 11%, healthcare at 7.7%, energy at 7.5%, and so on.

For GEQT, it is really those two sectors. Add industrials at 8.6% and healthcare at 6%, and you have the bulk of the portfolio. Both ETFs hold very little in communication services, consumer staples, utilities and real estate.

XEQT vs GEQT sector allocation

That 20-point gap matters if you are retired. A portfolio this concentrated can swing very fast.

What Do the Top Holdings Show?

GEQT leans on Nvidia and the Canadian banks. Its top 25 positions make up 39% of the ETF, against 28% for XEQT.

Both like Nvidia. It is about 3% of XEQT and 5.7% of GEQT.

In XEQT, the weights drop fast. Apple is near 3%, Microsoft at 2.4%, Royal Bank at 2%, then Amazon at 1.5%, and the 10th largest position, Bank of Montreal, sits at 0.85%.

GEQT looks completely different. TD Bank at 3.3%, Royal Bank at 3%, Broadcom and Shopify near 3% each, Bank of Montreal and Scotiabank near 2% each. Then Micron at 1.8%, CIBC at 1.74% and AMD at 1.49%. The theme is easy to see: financials and technology.

XEQT vs GEQT top 10 holdings

Three things stand out with GEQT. The big Nvidia weight. Zero Apple, Microsoft, Amazon or Alphabet. And no Meta or Tesla either, while XEQT holds all of them.

You can debate whether Apple or Microsoft are less ESG than Nvidia. I don’t have an opinion on that. You can ask yourself if it is worth it.

Even with 800 companies, GEQT’s top 25 is close to 40% of your money.

Which One Performed Better?

About the same so far. GEQT is slightly ahead since inception. In 2022, though, XEQT fell 11% and GEQT fell 15.7%.

2022 was a bad year for the stock market, and GEQT took the bigger hit. With 800 stocks, you might think it is well diversified. It isn’t diversified enough.

XEQT vs GEQT calendar year total returns since 2022

The big question is whether ESG beat the regular market, or whether GEQT simply holds more chip and semiconductor stocks. That is what has been driving the stock market lately, up and down.

Can These ETFs Pay for Your Retirement?

Not through the yield. Both pay well under 2%. The money comes from total return, and you sell units to create your income.

I covered this a few weeks ago on a Retirement Friday episode of The Moose on the Loose. Selling units works, and it can generate more income than focusing on income ETFs. The numbers prove it, even through a prolonged bear market like 2008.

Yearly distributions on $100,000 with XEQT and GEQT

In December, I will show Retirement Loop members step by step how selling units to generate income works, and why it holds up.

What Are the Risks?

Four of them. Both are 100% stocks. GEQT is concentrated. GEQT is small, which can widen the bid and ask spread. And both carry currency risk.

100% stocks. Right now it feels like unicorns and rainbows, with double digit returns every year. There is risk there, especially if you are retired. On my side, I will be 100% invested in stocks for the rest of my life. That’s just me. It isn’t necessarily you.

Concentration. 64% in two sectors is a bit too much for my taste. Again, that’s just me.

Liquidity. Check the bid and ask spread on any ETF. XEQT has $23.6 billion in assets, GEQT about $300 million. A smaller ETF can show a bigger spread, which matters for limit orders, and even more if you sell in a panic (which you should not do, but it happens).

Currency. Both trade in Canadian dollars. You still carry foreign currency risk through the US dollar, the euro and Asian currencies. Keep that in mind as you walk into retirement.

XEQT vs GEQT risks to watch

XEQT or GEQT: Which One Is Best for You?

It depends on the bet you want. XEQT buys the broad market. GEQT is a big bet on tech and financials built on an ESG screen.

Ask yourself three questions before you pick either one.

  • Do you want the broad market or a screened version of it? GEQT is the ESG version. With XEQT, you buy the world.

  • Are you comfortable with the concentration? If you like GEQT, you could pair it with something else to lower the exposure to tech and financials.

  • What is your investment objective? Are you comfortable managing a portfolio built on total return, and generating your own income in retirement? If yes, both are great products. If not, you might want to add fixed income, more dividend-paying stocks or another strategy.

The key is always the same. Find a strategy you understand, one you are comfortable with, and one you will stick to when your portfolio is down 10%. That is how you live a happy retirement.

Build Your Retirement Income Plan Before Christmas

Once you pick your ETF, the next question is how to turn it into a paycheck for the rest of your life.

Retirement Loop is my community for Canadians who want to build and follow their own retirement plan. The doors are open now. In December, members get the full webinar on selling units to generate income, step by step.

data.title: Nvidia Doubled Revenue. P/E Fell To A 10-Year Low
data.description:
"Our momentum is real," Colette Kress said on 17 November, in her first results release as Nvidia's (NVDA) interim CEO. The figures backed her up. Revenue more than doubled in a year, to $115.8 billion, and the forecast for the current quarter came in above what analysts expected. The next day the shares fell 2.9%.

That is Nvidia's puzzle right now. The company earns more every quarter, and the market pays less for each dollar of it. At the 18 November close Nvidia traded at its lowest multiple of earnings in at least ten years. The report itself explains a good part of why.

Rubin's record start

In the three months to 25 October, Nvidia sold nearly twice as much as in all of fiscal 2024. Data center sales, the chips, networking and systems that train and run AI models, came to $107.6 billion of it, up 110%.

Much of the jump came from Vera Rubin, the rack-scale system that began shipping in the quarter. Kress told analysts it brought in nearly $20 billion in its first quarter, the fastest ramp in Nvidia's history. Networking, the gear that links thousands of chips into one machine, passed $21 billion.

The rest of Nvidia, now reported as Edge Computing, grew 42% to $8.2 billion on workstations and chips for robots and cars, while higher memory prices weighed on gaming PCs.

Nvidia revenue by customer

Nvidia splits its data center sales by customer, and the split tells a new story. Sales to hyperscale customers, the giant cloud and internet platforms, rose 71% to $60.1 billion. Sales to everyone else, a group of AI clouds, industrial companies and enterprises, nearly tripled to $47.5 billion.

A year ago that second group was under a third of data center sales. Now it is 44%. A longer customer list spreads Nvidia's risk, and it also brings in buyers with far less cash of their own than Microsoft or Amazon, the AI cloud start-ups above all.

How the buildout gets paid for

Those newer buyers need money, and Nvidia increasingly provides the backing. Its $32 billion of agreements with neoclouds, the young AI cloud companies, depend on those partners raising financing. It has also agreed to guarantee up to $105 billion of credit support for SB Energy's campus in Ohio, which will host Nvidia systems under 20-year leases to OpenAI.

Customers are paying more slowly, too. Money owed to Nvidia for chips already delivered rose to $81 billion, and the average customer now takes 64 days to pay, up from 60 a quarter earlier. Nvidia puts part of that down to longer payment terms on large multi-quarter deals with some investment-grade customers.

The cash still pours in. Free cash flow nearly doubled, and Nvidia returned a record $28.1 billion to shareholders, $22.1 billion of it through buybacks.

Nvidia's biggest customers already lean on borrowing, as we wrote in Nvidia's Biggest Customers Keep Spending. Power and Debt Set the Limits. Now the supplier stands behind part of the bill as well.

Why Nvidia stock fell after earnings

Then the price went the other way. Nvidia's earnings per share over the last four quarters rose 130% on a year earlier. Over the same year the share price fell 17%, and at the 18 November close it sat 37% below its record on 6 October.

Put those two together and the multiple collapses. Nvidia traded at 16x its trailing earnings, below every month-end reading of the past ten years. The low before this was 18x, in December 2018, and the ten-year median is 54x.

Two things explain much of the latest drop. The first sits at the top. Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and ran it from the start, resigned as CEO on 12 November, and the filing gave no reason. Kress runs the company until the board names a successor, Harvey Jones became its first chair, and an independent board committee is still investigating. On the earnings call the board ruled out bringing Huang back. From the last close before the news, the shares lost 13%.

The second is the forecast. The quarter to January has an extra week, so per week $130 billion is only about 4% above this quarter's pace, by our arithmetic, after 20% growth from the quarter before.

The forecast excludes data center compute revenue from China, compared with $2.4 billion of shipments there this quarter, and gross margin is guided down to 71% to 72% as Rubin ramps. Kress still expects revenue to grow about 75% next fiscal year.

How much Nvidia is in the S&P 500 and other ETFs

Most investors own Nvidia through a fund, and how much they own depends on which one. It is about 6% of both SPY, the S&P 500 fund, and QQQ, the Nasdaq-100 fund. Growth and tech funds hold more: about 10% of VUG, Vanguard's growth fund, and 14% of VGT, its tech fund.

Of these funds, the biggest share sits in SMH, VanEck's chip fund, at 17%. SOXX, the iShares chip fund, holds about 7%, because its index caps the weight of its largest companies.

That share is the lever. With everything else unchanged, a 10% move in Nvidia moves SPY by about 0.6% and SMH by about 1.7%.

The P/E here is the share price over the last four quarters of reported earnings per share; the fund shares are our look-through of each fund's holdings at the 18 November close.

Kress called the momentum real, and the report agrees. What the market will pay for it has not been this low in ten years.

data.title: Bitcoin ETFs Lose $975M In A Week As Russia Moves To Open Bitcoin To Funds
data.description:
S spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) lost a net 4,658 BTC, about $296.7 million, in their latest daily update, on-chain tracker Lookonchain reported on Thursday, November 19. Over seven days, the funds shed 15,314 BTC, or $975.5 million. All five of the largest funds posted outflows on both the day and the week.

On the same day, Russia moved the other way. A Bank of Russia official said the central bank plans rule changes that would let investment funds for qualified investors buy Bitcoin directly, with the first products possible in 2027. Retail access to crypto futures is also being weighed, but later.

We compared the week’s ETF selling with the new coins miners produced over the same days. The selling was almost five times larger. So, can new buyers like Russia fill a gap this big?

Bitcoin ETFs: Every Major Fund Saw Outflows This Week

Lookonchain’s table shows the selling was broad, not limited to one issuer:

  • BlackRock (IBIT): -2,377 BTC on the day and -9,417 BTC over the week, about 61% of the weekly total. It still holds 778,966 BTC, the largest stash by far.

  • Fidelity (FBTC): -1,109 BTC on the day and -2,348 BTC over the week.

  • Grayscale (GBTC and BTC): -265 BTC on the day and -1,455 BTC over the week.

  • Bitwise (BITB) and ARK 21Shares (ARKB): -586 and -308 BTC on the day, -955 and -838 BTC over the week.

Together, the US funds now hold 1,231,539 BTC, worth about $78.45 billion. The week’s outflows equal about 1.2% of that.

Ethereum ETFs saw the same pattern on a smaller scale. They lost 9,904 ETH, about $17.9 million, on the day. Over the week, outflows reached 65,373 ETH, or $117.8 million. BlackRock’s ETHA accounted for most of it.

US BTC ETF Selling Was 4.8 Times the New Supply

Every day, miners create new BTC as a reward for adding blocks to the network. We counted the blocks added in the seven days to Thursday afternoon UTC on mempool.space, a public block explorer: 1,030 blocks at 3.125 BTC each, or about 3,219 new BTC.

  • The gap: ETF outflows of 15,314 BTC were 4.8 times the BTC miners produced in the same week.

  • What it means: when investors pull money from an ETF, the fund gives up coins to pay them back, and most of it ends up sold in the market. Other buyers have to absorb that on top of what miners sell.

  • The price: BTC fell from about $74,000 on November 11 to a low near $62,000 on November 15. It trades near $64,000 now.

This is where Russia’s plan looks small for now. From November 17, ordinary Russian investors can buy BTC through licensed brokers and exchanges, but only up to 300,000 rubles a year per intermediary. That’s about $3,670, or roughly 0.057 BTC at today’s price. It would take about 267,000 Russians buying the full amount to match one week of US ETF selling.

Russia’s Bitcoin Plan: Funds First, Retail Futures Later

Russia legalized regulated crypto trading this year, and the rules are rolling out in steps:

  • Retail spot access: since November 17, retail investors can buy BTC, ETH and USDT after passing a knowledge test. The rules come from a Bank of Russia ordinance that sets the 300,000-ruble yearly cap. Qualified investors, who meet wealth or experience thresholds, have no cap.

  • Qualified funds: Olga Shishlyannikova, who heads the central bank’s department for investment intermediaries, spoke on November 18. She said the bank is considering rule changes next year to let funds for qualified investors buy crypto. Today, those funds can only use derivatives that pay out in cash. The first products could come in 2027, once the changes are registered with the Ministry of Justice.

  • Retail funds and futures: funds for ordinary investors are not part of the plan for now, and retail access to crypto futures is only being weighed, with no timeline.

  • Next steps: Moscow Exchange plans to start crypto trading on December 1, and direct peer-to-peer crypto trades are set to end in July 2027.

For Bitcoin, Russia is a long-term story. Regulated funds could add steady demand from 2027, but none of it arrives in time to offset this month’s ETF selling.

Bitcoin Price Analysis: $62,300 Has Held Twice

On the daily chart, Bitcoin trades at $64,037. That is below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $75,258, and its 200-day EMA at $75,627.

  • Support: $62,300, where BTC bounced on November 15 and 18, after holding in February, June, July and August. Below that, $57,800, the July low.

  • Resistance: $65,500, a level that turned BTC back in June, July and August. Above that, $74,300.

BTCUSDT 1D chart. Source: TradingView

For Bitcoin, the number to watch is the daily ETF flow. A few days of inflows would ease the pressure on $62,300. Another week like this one, with outflows near five times new supply, would make that support much harder to defend.

data.description:
Last Friday, we described that day’s activity as a “rug pull.”  On that day, we saw stocks rise in the pre-market and on the open, then sink quickly afterwards.  Today, we’re seeing something similar, though after a much bigger early rally.  Traders were clearly enthusiastic about the prospects for the much-awaited IPO[i] (it has still not opened as I type this), but that stock’s coattails were not long enough to drag the whole market along with it this morning.

The charts below show the dramatic moves in both ES (E-Mini S&P 500) and NQ (Nasdaq 100 E-Mini) December Futures.  At their highs, ES was up about 1.4% around 6:55 ET, and NQ was up about 2.4% around 9:50. Soon afterwards, those gains reversed quite abruptly.  The S&P 500 (SPX) gravitated once again toward the 7,300 level that has provided support over the past three sessions, while the Nasdaq 100 (NDX) spent very little time in negative territory.

ES December Futures, 2 Days, 2 Minute Candles

But now it finds itself struggling to hold current support. Last week's spike low (from the bullish hammer) is set to be negated as a reversal candlestick, but there is an aggressive buy with a very tight stop (loss of $62K) as I have seen recoveries from similar situations in the past. But this is crash territory and there isn't a whole lot of support below $57.5K

The S&P loss 7,250 support as part of the 200-day MA undercut. Technicals are net negative and oversold. There is still a chance for a 'bear' trap, but as other indices move away from support it becomes harder to see this leading a recovery, but that shouldn't discount the possibility; a move above 7.25K would confirm a 'bear trap'.

It's not all doom-and-gloom. The equal-weighted S&P took a big hit, but it's still range bound, so losses remain noise within the larger trading range. Technicals are net negative but it hasn't yet challenged its 200-day MA or range support, so if the index can hold on it may yet take on a leadership role on the next recovery.

data.title: Why State Governments May Matter More Than Congress For Energy Policy
data.description:
The 2026 midterm elections produced a major political shift in Washington. Democrats will control both chambers of Congress when the new session begins in January, during President Donald Trump’s final two years in the White House. 

That combination almost guarantees more conflict over energy policy, but it does not necessarily mean sweeping changes in federal law. The more consequential changes may occur somewhere else.

Governors, state legislatures, and utility commissions have substantial authority over where power plants and transmission lines are built, what utilities can charge customers, how large new electricity users are treated, and how environmental and water permits are issued. The election changed control of several of those institutions, including in states experiencing rapid growth in electricity demand. As a result, the most important energy-policy consequences of the midterms may emerge state by state rather than through another major act of Congress.

Washington Is Likely to Be a Check

Democrats are projected to enter the next Congress with at least 255 House seats and 55 Senate seats. That gives them control over committees, oversight, appropriations, and Senate confirmations. But President Trump retains the veto, and most Senate legislation will still require 60 votes unless it can move through a special procedure such as budget reconciliation.

The practical result is that neither side can easily impose a comprehensive new energy agenda. Democrats can challenge Trump administration policies on federal leasing, LNG, mining, coal, and environmental regulation, while the administration can block legislation attempting to reverse much of what it has done since 2025. Control of the Senate will give Democrats leverage over future nominees to energy and environmental agencies, while congressional committees will gain much greater ability to investigate administration decisions.

There may still be areas of bipartisan agreement, particularly permitting reform. But that subject has already become more complicated following the election, with some Democrats debating whether to accept a bipartisan permitting package now or wait until they control Congress and try to renegotiate it. 

The Senate voted 73-25 on November 14 to move forward with the American Affordability and Jobs Act, which would accelerate permitting for power plants, transmission lines, mines, and other infrastructure while addressing some of the grid costs associated with large data centers.

In other words, Washington is still relevant. But divided government makes it more likely that the next two years will be defined by bargaining, oversight, and selective compromise than by another major rewrite of U.S. energy policy.

The States Have Much More Room to Move

The picture is very different at the state level.

The election created six new Democratic trifectas, meaning one party will control the governor’s office and both legislative chambers, in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. Republican trifectas were broken in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas. As of November 12, eleven states had changed their governing alignment as a result of the election.

Those changes have direct implications for energy because state governments make decisions that federal policy often cannot reach. Utility commissions approve generation and transmission investments. Governors appoint regulators in many states. Legislatures establish renewable requirements, tax incentives, and rules governing large electricity users. Environmental agencies issue permits, while state and local governments determine how much control communities have over industrial development.

That authority has become particularly important because the fastest-growing energy-policy issue in many states is no longer a traditional fight over coal versus renewables. It is the explosive growth of data centers and the electricity, transmission, and water infrastructure required to support them.

The political question increasingly is who pays for that growth.

Pennsylvania Is Already Changing the Rules

Pennsylvania provides a good example of how state  energy policy can move even when federal policy is stalled.

Governor Josh Shapiro issued an executive order in August establishing new requirements for data-center projects seeking state permits and tax benefits. Developers are expected to bear the full cost of new generation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure needed to serve their projects rather than shifting those costs to other customers. The requirements also address water conservation, disclosure, community engagement, and local approval.

The election gives Democrats unified control of Pennsylvania government, potentially allowing some of those policies to move beyond executive action and into statute. That could affect not only data-center development but also the type of generation built to meet rapidly growing power demand.

Pennsylvania occupies an unusual position in the U.S. energy system. It is one of the country’s largest natural-gas producers and sits inside PJM, the nation’s largest grid operator. PJM has already been struggling with tightening reserve margins, slow additions of new generation and transmission, and rapidly increasing electricity demand. Policies that alter where data centers locate, who pays for new infrastructure, or how quickly new generation is permitted can therefore have consequences far beyond Pennsylvania’s borders.

This is one reason the state-level story should not be reduced to whether Democrats favor renewable energy and Republicans favor fossil fuels. Pennsylvania needs more electricity. The harder questions concern what kind of generation gets built, how quickly it can be connected, and who absorbs the cost.

Utility Commissions Could Be Even More Important

Some of the most consequential election results received relatively little national attention because they involved utility regulators rather than governors or members of Congress.

Georgia is a good example. Democrats won control of the five-member Georgia Public Service Commission, which regulates Georgia Power and approves many of the utility’s major investments. Georgia has historically been viewed as one of the more constructive regulatory environments for utilities, but the new commission is likely to place greater emphasis on affordability and the costs associated with the state’s enormous data-center buildout.

Southern Company said during its third-quarter earnings call that Georgia Power has approximately 14.5 gigawatts of contracted data-center load. That is an enormous amount of potential demand, and the Public Service Commission will have a direct role in determining how the generation and grid investments required to serve that load are approved and financed.

This distinction is important for investors. A utility may have enormous opportunities to invest in new generation and transmission, but the value of that investment depends heavily on the regulatory compact. Who pays? What return is allowed? How much cost can be recovered from large-load customers instead of residential ratepayers? Those questions are often decided by a five-member state commission rather than Congress.

Arizona is moving in a similar direction. Democrats won two seats on the Arizona Corporation Commission, although Republicans will retain a 3-2 majority. The commission regulates electric, gas, and water utilities, giving it significant influence over both electricity costs and water issues associated with large new industrial loads.

At the same time, Democrats gained control of the Arizona Legislature while Gov. Katie Hobbs won reelection, creating a Democratic trifecta. Data-center policy is already emerging as one of its first internal debates. Some Democratic legislators and Attorney General Kris Mayes favor a temporary moratorium, while Hobbs has rejected that approach but remains open to stronger regulation involving water use, tax incentives, and protection of existing utility customers.

The disagreement is revealing. Even within the same party, the choice is not simply between welcoming development and opposing it. Arizona wants investment and jobs, but it also faces serious water constraints and rapidly increasing demand for electricity. The policy debate is increasingly about the terms under which development occurs.

Texas May Be the Most Interesting Case

Texas probably provides the best example of why the election’s  energy consequences cannot be reduced to conventional partisan assumptions.

Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Gov. Greg Abbott, Democrats captured the Texas House for the first time since 2003, and Democrat Vikki Goodwin defeated Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick. Republicans, however, retained a 19-12 majority in the Texas Senate. The result is divided government rather than a Democratic trifecta.

That makes a dramatic reversal of Texas oil and gas policy unlikely. The industry remains central to the state’s economy, and the Republican Senate will be a significant constraint on legislation. But several areas could change substantially.

Data centers are the most obvious. Abbott had already halted state permitting for data centers while ERCOT evaluated their impact on the grid and water supplies. Hinojosa campaigned on extending that pause until lawmakers establish stronger protections involving electricity costs, water use, tax subsidies, transparency, and local control.

The governor will also gain influence over the Public Utility Commission of Texas through appointments as terms expire. That commission plays a major role in ERCOT market policy, transmission investment, and the treatment of large new electricity users. FactSet notes that upcoming vacancies could give Hinojosa substantial ability to reshape the commission over time, even though those changes would not occur overnight.

Then there is the Texas Railroad Commission, which despite its name regulates the state’s enormous oil and gas industry.

Democrat Jon Rosenthal became the first member of his party elected to the commission in more than three decades. But he will remain in the minority alongside two Republican commissioners, limiting his ability to impose broad regulatory changes.

What makes Rosenthal interesting is that his agenda does not fit into the usual political caricature. He spent about 25 years as an oil-field engineer and has said he wants to streamline permitting for responsible operators, increase oil and gas production, improve agency staffing, and accelerate the plugging of orphan wells. He has also advocated stronger pollution enforcement, changes in wastewater-disposal policy, and greater transparency at the commission.

That combination may be a better indication of where state energy politics are heading than the traditional argument over whether government is “for” or “against” fossil fuels. Texas can remain the country’s dominant oil and gas producer while changing how the industry is regulated, how abandoned wells are handled, and how the environmental costs of production are assigned.

Data Centers Are Rewriting the Energy Debate

The common thread running through Pennsylvania, Georgia, Arizona, and Texas is the rapid growth of data centers.

The issue played a large role in the 2026 elections. Candidates in numerous states called for tougher rules governing electricity costs, water consumption, tax incentives, and local approval. Voters also approved many local restrictions on data-center development.

Nevada, even before the election, adopted a framework requiring data centers receiving state incentives to bear the cost of serving their electricity demand, comply with water standards and avoid shifting grid costs to other customers. Pennsylvania has adopted a similar principle, while candidates in Arizona, Georgia, and Texas campaigned on variations of the same idea.

That represents a meaningful change in the energy-policy debate. For much of the past two decades, national energy politics revolved around climate policy, drilling, pipelines, and renewable-energy mandates. Those issues have not disappeared, but electricity affordability and infrastructure are moving rapidly toward the center of the discussion.

The questions are increasingly practical. How many new power plants will be required? Who pays for transmission? Can water supplies support new development? Should residential customers subsidize infrastructure built primarily for large technology companies? And can projects move through permitting quickly enough to meet demand without bypassing local concerns?

Those are largely state and regulatory questions.

The Big Picture

The 2026 elections will certainly alter the tone of federal energy policy. Congress will investigate more, the administration will face greater resistance, and bipartisan legislation will require more negotiation. But divided government makes sweeping federal change difficult.

The states are where things could get more interesting.

New governors, legislative majorities, and utility commissioners now have direct authority over decisions that determine whether projects get built, how quickly they proceed, and who ultimately pays for them. Some of those changes could encourage cleaner generation or stronger environmental oversight. Others may accelerate conventional  energy development while placing tougher conditions on water use, infrastructure costs, or abandoned wells.

That is why the most important energy consequence of the 2026 election may not be a new law coming out of Washington. It may be dozens of decisions in state capitols and regulatory hearing rooms that gradually determine where the next power plant, transmission line, data center, or energy project gets built.

data.title: EU Lawmakers, States Agree To 2-Year Delay To Methane Reporting Rules
data.description:
Lawmakers in the European Parliament and EU Member States announced that they reached a provisional agreement to postpone methane monitoring and reporting rules for oil, gas and coal importers by two years, supporting an EU Commission proposal aimed at avoiding adding pressure to the EU’s security of energy supply.

While extending the delay beyond the Commission’s initial one-year proposal, the agreement marks a compromise between Parliament’s and the European Council’s positions going into negotiations of a 3-year and 1-year postponement, respectively.

Rapid reduction in methane emissions is seen as one of the most effective near-term actions that can be taken to help achieve the global climate goal to limit warming to 1.5°C. Methane is an extremely potent greenhouse gas (GHG), with as much as 80x the warming power of CO2, and oil and gas facilities are among the largest industrial sources of methane emissions.

The EU adopted a new law in 2024 setting rules for measuring, reporting and verifying methane emissions, for finding and repairing leaks, and for limiting venting and flaring, representing the world’s first comprehensive legislation to regulate methane emissions related to imports of oil, gas and coal.

The requirements for monitoring, reporting and verification for natural gas, oil and coal importers are currently set to begin in 2028, but in October the Commission proposed a one-year delay, citing a need to help avoid additional pressures on the security of supply of imported fossil fuels in the current geopolitical context.

Parliament adopted its negotiating position in October, proposing to extend the delay to 2031, noting that importers have warned that they may not be able to secure enough compliant supplies, with energy markets already strained. Council’s position aligned with the Commission’s 1-year delay, but added a requirement for the Commission to assess by September 30, 2027 whether the necessary elements for the implementation of the reporting obligations are met, including a sufficient number of third-party verifiers to assess the conformity of the emission reports, and whether there are in place EU implementing rules on transferring information about methane emissions between producers and importers, as well as on equivalent third-party verification and monitoring procedures in third countries.

The compromise agreement, which still requires endorsement by Parliament and the Council, would delay the rules by 2 years, with monitoring, reporting and verification obligations for natural gas, crude oil and coal importers beginning in January 2029, while also maintaining the Council’s requirements, including requiring the Commission to review the effective implementation of the methane regulation by the beginning of January 2028.

The fixed 1:1 rate can apply whether users switch to a different stablecoin or move the same token to another blockchain. On a supported cross-chain USDT-to-USDC route, for example, a user sending 10,000 USDT receives exactly 10,000 USDC.
